title: A. A Simple Sequence
statement:
You are given an integer $$n$$. You need to construct a permutation$$^{∗}$$ $$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$ using integers from $$1$$ to $$n$$ such that the following condition is satisfied:

$$$ a_1 \bmod a_2 $\geq a_2 \bmod a_3 \geq \ldots \geq a_{n-1} \bmod a_{n}, $$$$ where $$u$$ mod $$v$$ denotes the remainder of dividing $$u$$ by $$v$$.

If multiple valid permutations exist, you may output any of them.

It can be shown that a valid permutation always exists for every $$n $\geq 2$$$.

$$^{∗}$$A permutation of length $$n$$ is an array consisting of $$n$$ distinct integers from $$1$$ to $$n$$ in arbitrary order. For example, $$[2,3,1,5,4]$$ is a permutation, but $$[1,2,2]$$ is not a permutation ($$2$$ appears twice in the array), and $$[1,3,4]$$ is also not a permutation ($$n=3$$ but there is $$4$$ in the array).

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$t$$ ($$1 $\leq t \leq 100$$$). The description of the test cases follows.

The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$n$$ ($$2 $\leq n \leq 100$$$).

For each test case, output on a single line $$n$$ space-separated integers $$a_1, a_2, \ldots a_n$$.

If multiple valid permutations exist, you may output any of them.

In the second test case, $$2 \bmod 3 $\geq 3 \bmod 1$$$, so the permutation $$[2, 3, 1]$$ is valid.

In the third test case, $$2 \bmod 4 $\geq 4 \bmod 3 \geq 3 \bmod 1$$$, so the permutation $$[2, 4, 3, 1]$$ is valid.

output: Output For each test case, output on a single line $$n$$ space-separated integers $$a_1, a_2, \ldots a_n$$. If multiple valid permutations exist, you may output any of them.
